q: How many sections of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 does the lecture list?
explain: The slide lists Section 1, Section 2, Section 3, Section 3ZA and Section 3A.
flag: A past-test style question asks about "levels of offences". The slide gives five sections, but penalties are given for only three, S1, S2 and S3. Check which count the question means.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised access to computer material?
explain: Section 1 covers UNAUTHORISED access to computer material.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate commission of further offences?
explain: Section 2 covers UNAUTHORISED access with intent to commit or facilitate commission of further offences.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised acts with intent to impair, or with recklessness as to impairing, operation of a computer?
explain: Section 3 covers UNAUTHORISED acts with intent to impair, or with recklessness as to impairing, operation of computer.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers unauthorised acts causing, or creating risk of, serious damage?
explain: Section 3ZA covers UNAUTHORISED acts causing, or creating risk of, serious damage.

q: Which section of the Computer Misuse Act 1990 covers making, supplying or obtaining articles for use in an offence under section 1, 2, 3 or 3ZA?
explain: Section 3A covers making, supplying or obtaining articles for use in an offence under section 1, 2, 3 or 3ZA.

q: What is the maximum prison term for a Section 1 offence under the slides?
explain: A Section 1 offence carries a fine or 2 years in prison, or both. The previous limit was 6 months.
flag: The slide gives no penalty for 3ZA or 3A. In real law S1 is up to 2 years on indictment and 6 months on summary conviction.

q: What was the previous maximum prison term for a Section 1 offence before it was raised to 2 years?
explain: A Section 1 offence carries a fine or 2 years in prison, or both. The previous limit was 6 months.

q: What is the maximum prison term for a Section 2 offence under the slides?
explain: A Section 2 offence carries a fine or 5 years in prison, or both.

q: What is the maximum prison term for a Section 3 offence under the slides?
explain: A Section 3 offence carries a fine or 10 years in prison, or both.

q: Which Act of 1990 sets out the offences of unauthorised access to computer material and unauthorised acts with intent to impair a computer?
explain: Computer Misuse Act 1990, Sections 1, 2, 3, 3ZA and 3A.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Laws come from moral attitudes or customs
Ethics carry the authority of a governing body
Law is not drawn from ethics
explain: Ethics define socially acceptable behaviours. Laws are drawn from ethics and carry the authority of a governing body, and ethics come from moral attitudes or customs.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Ethics carry the authority of a governing body
Laws carry the authority of a governing body
Laws come from moral attitudes or customs
Ethics are rules that mandate or prohibit certain behaviour
explain: The main differences are that laws carry the authority of a governing body and ethics come from moral attitudes or customs.

q: Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Both ethics and laws are always local
Both ethics and laws are always universal
Laws can be universal, whereas ethics tend to be local
Ethics can be universal, whereas laws tend to be local
explain: Ethics can be universal, laws tend to be local.

q: Which of the following statements about laws is correct?
options: Laws are rules that mandate or prohibit certain behaviour and are drawn from ethics
Laws are guidelines that describe acceptable and unacceptable behaviour
Laws are not drawn from ethics
explain: Laws are rules that mandate or prohibit certain behaviour and are drawn from ethics. Policy is guidelines.

q: Which statement about policy vs law is correct?
options: A policy carries the authority of a governing body
A policy has no penalties for non-compliance
explain: The main differences are that ignoring a policy is acceptable and ignoring a law is unacceptable.
flag: The slide says policy "has penalties for non-compliance" yet also "ignoring a policy is acceptable", and these sit awkwardly together. Follow the slide wording.

q: According to the slides, which describes a policy?
options: Behaviours that are socially acceptable, defined by custom
Guidelines that describe acceptable and unacceptable behaviour, with penalties for non-compliance
Rules that mandate or prohibit certain behaviour, drawn from ethics
Standards that carry the authority of a governing body
explain: A policy is guidelines that describe acceptable and unacceptable behaviour, and it has penalties for non-compliance.

q: In business law, what is 'due care'?
options: The organisation reports all breaches to the ICO
The organisation makes sure employees know what is acceptable or unacceptable
The organisation makes a valid effort to protect employees, customers etc.
The organisation hires a reputable auditor
explain: Due care is when the organisation makes sure employees know what is acceptable or unacceptable.

q: In business law, what is 'due diligence'?
options: The organisation publishes its terms and conditions
The organisation makes a valid effort to protect employees, customers etc.
The organisation hires an ethical hacker
The organisation makes sure employees know what is acceptable or unacceptable
explain: Due diligence is when the organisation makes a valid effort to protect employees, customers etc.

q: Which description matches cyber-dependent crime?
options: Crimes that can be committed only through the use of ICT devices, where the devices are both the tool and the target of the crime
Crimes committed only by organised crime groups
Any crime in which a computer holds evidence
Traditional crimes which can be increased in scale or reach by the use of computers
explain: Cyber-dependent crimes can be committed only through ICT devices, where the devices are both the tool for committing the crime, and the target of the crime.

q: Which description matches cyber-enabled crime?
options: Crimes that can be committed only through the use of ICT devices
Traditional crimes which can be increased in scale or reach by the use of computers, computer networks or other forms of ICT
Crimes where the device is both the tool and the target
Crimes that need malware to be committed
explain: Cyber-enabled crimes are traditional crimes which can be increased in scale or reach by the use of computers, computer networks or other forms of ICT.

q: Which of the following is an example of a cyber-dependent crime?
explain: Cyber-dependent crime is illicit intrusion into networks or disrupting a service, for example hacking, defacing a website, DoS and malware. Cyberstalking, grooming and piracy are cyber-enabled.

q: Which of the following is an example of a cyber-enabled crime?
explain: Cyber-enabled crimes include offenses against a specific target - cyberstalking. DoS, malware and defacing are cyber-dependent.

q: Which Act, dated 2000, is listed with the Computer Misuse Act 1990 under cyber-dependent crime?
explain: The cyber-dependent crimes slide lists the Computer Misuse Act 1990, the Regulation of Investigation Powers Act 2000 and the Data Protection Act 1998.
flag: The slide spells it "Regulation of Investigation Powers Act", and the real title is Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000.

q: Which Act, dated 1998, is listed with the Computer Misuse Act 1990 under cyber-dependent crime?
explain: The slide lists the Data Protection Act 1998, which has some civil and some criminal offences.

q: Which Act does the lecture say may be easier to prove to the criminal standard of proof than the Computer Misuse Act?
explain: Other Acts, for example the Fraud Act 2006, may be easier to prove to the criminal standard of proof.

q: What does the Gary McKinnon case illustrate in the lecture?
options: The need for PCI DSS compliance
explain: There are often jurisdictional problems, especially cross border, for example the long running saga of Gary McKinnon.

q: What is required for penetration testing so the tester does not get arrested?
options: An authorisation letter from a genuine high level manager (e.g. an IT Director) who has the authority to give it
A verbal agreement from any employee
explain: It is easy to get arrested, so the tester needs an authorisation letter from a genuine high level manager who has the authority to give it, for example an IT Director, and that person must be present to verify it.

q: Which type of attacker breaks into networks to discover weaknesses in order to improve their security?
explain: White hat attackers break into networks or computer systems to discover weaknesses in order to improve the security of these systems.

q: Which type of attacker may report a vulnerability to the owners of the system if that action coincides with their agenda?
explain: Gray hat attackers ... may find a vulnerability and report it to the owners of the system if that action coincides with their agenda.

q: Which type of attacker is described as an unethical criminal who violates computer and network security for personal gain or malicious reasons?
explain: Black hat attackers are unethical criminals who violate computer and network security for personal gain, or for malicious reasons.

q: What does PCI DSS stand for?
options: Personal Card Information Data Safety Standard
Payment Card Internet Digital Security Scheme
Public Credit Industry Data Safety Standard
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard
explain: PCI DSS stands for Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard.

q: PCI DSS was the result of collaboration between which groups?
options: The UK Government and the ICO
Credit card companies such as American Express, MasterCard and VISA
explain: PCI DSS resulted from collaboration between credit card companies such as American Express, MasterCard and VISA.

q: If you lose card data under PCI DSS compliance, whom must you declare it to?
explain: If you lose card data you must declare it to ICO.

q: Which Act requires US public companies to set up 'hotlines' so employees can anonymously raise concerns about accounting or audit irregularities?
explain: Under Sarbanes Oxley, known as SOX, US public companies must establish procedures called "hotlines". EuroSOX is the EU equivalent.

q: What is EuroSOX?
options: A UK law on card data
The EU equivalent of PCI DSS
The EU equivalent of Sarbanes Oxley
The EU equivalent of the Computer Misuse Act
explain: EuroSOX - EU equivalent.

q: What is 'Herod's clause' used to illustrate?
options: That PCI DSS must be treated as law
That hacking is a cross-border crime
That nobody reads terms and conditions, which are nevertheless legally binding
explain: Terms and conditions are legally binding, so how do you enforce them when no one reads them? Herod's clause illustrates this, citing the Guardian in 2014.

q: Which body is part of the National Crime Agency (NCA)?
explain: The National Cyber Crime Unit is the police and is part of the National Crime Agency, the NCA.

q: Which body collaborates with Regional Organised Crime Units (ROCUs) to reduce cybercrime?
explain: The NCCU works with Regional Organised Crime Units, the ROCUs. Its job is to respond to threats and collaborate with partners to reduce cyber crime.

q: Which government body's main responsibility is to protect UK critical services from cyber attacks?
explain: The NCSC's job is to protect UK critical services from cyber attacks, manage major incidents and improve the security of the UK Internet.

q: GCHQ has the responsibility to:
options: Test and set standards for technology
Protect UK critical services from cyber attacks
Defend Government systems from cyber threat
explain: GCHQ protects the UK, with law enforcement and other intelligence agencies, and defends Government systems from cyber threat.

q: What does NCSC stand for?
explain: NCSC stands for National Cyber Security Centre.

q: Which body is described as an independent authority to which you report a DPA/GDPR breach?
explain: The ICO is an independent authority, and it is where you report a DPA or GDPR breach.

q: Which statement is correct about NIST?
options: It is a UK police unit within the NCA
It is the UK independent authority for data protection
It is a non-regulatory US agency that tests and sets standards for technology including security
It is a global not-for-profit supporting application security
explain: NIST, the National Institute for Standards and Technology, is a non-regulatory US agency that tests and sets standards for technology including security.

q: Which body is a global not-for-profit that supports application security through research, pen-testing and education?
options: National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST)
explain: OWASP is a global not-for-profit that supports application security through research, pen-testing and education.

q: Which body is a not-for-profit representing the information security industry and linked on the slide to 'CyberEssentials' professional qualifications?
explain: CREST is a not-for-profit organisation representing the information security industry, with research, pen-testing and education. The slide links it to "CyberEssentials" professional qualifications.

q: Where does the lecture say to report a cybercrime?
explain: Report a cybercrime at www.actionfraud.police.uk.

q: Under PCI DSS, which goal includes 'use and regularly update anti-virus software'?
options: Build and Maintain a Secure Network
explain: Goal 3 is Maintain a Vulnerability Management Program, which covers using and regularly updating anti-virus software and developing and maintaining secure systems and applications.

q: Under PCI DSS, which goal includes 'assign a unique ID to each person with computer access'?
explain: Goal 4 is Implement Strong Access Control Measures. It covers restricting access to data by business need-to-know, assigning a unique ID to each person with computer access, and restricting physical access to cardholder data.

q: Which is NOT one of the six PCI DSS goals?
options: Report all card data losses to the NCA
Build and Maintain a Secure Network
explain: The six goals are a secure network, protecting cardholder data, a vulnerability management programme, strong access control, regularly monitoring and testing networks, and an information security policy.

q: What are the main challenges in prosecuting crimes under the CMA?
options: Proof that the defendant was the perpetrator
Proof of offence (e.g. logs/audit trails) and that the computer was working properly
Irrelevant technical detail baffling the judge or jury
explain: Slide 15 lists these problems in prosecuting.

q: What are the main challenges in prosecuting crimes under the CMA?
options: Technical detail baffling a judge or jury
Hacking is only an offence under the Data Protection Act
Proof that the defendant was the perpetrator
The Act only applies to US companies
explain: The problems in prosecuting are proving unauthorised access, intent, the offence and logs, the perpetrator, and technical detail baffling a judge or jury.

q: PCI DSS sets out ways to:
options: Report data breaches to the NCA
explain: PCI DSS sets out ways to protect card holder data, securely transfer card holder data and monitor your own network.

q: Which of the following are PCI DSS goals?
options: Build and Maintain a Secure Network
explain: Slides 17-18 list these six goals.

q: Which of the following are PCI DSS goals?
explain: The six goals are a secure network, protecting cardholder data, a vulnerability management programme, strong access control, regularly monitoring and testing, and an information security policy.

q: Under PCI DSS 'Implement Strong Access Control Measures', which of the following apply?
options: Restrict physical access to cardholder data
Restrict access to data by business need-to-know
Assign a unique ID to each person with computer access
Use vendor-supplied defaults for system passwords
Share one login among a team
explain: Goal 4, Implement Strong Access Control Measures, covers need-to-know access, a unique ID, and restricting physical access.

q: Under PCI DSS 'Protect Cardholder Data' and 'Build and Maintain a Secure Network', which of the following apply?
options: Do not use vendor-supplied defaults for system passwords and other security parameters
Install and maintain a firewall configuration to protect data
Use vendor-supplied defaults for system passwords
Encrypt transmission of cardholder data and sensitive information across public net
Send cardholder data in plain text across public networks
explain: Goals 1 and 2 on slide 17.

q: Which of the following are cyber-enabled crimes?
explain: Cyber-enabled crime covers economic crime such as fraud, piracy, IP theft and forgery, cyberstalking, and child sexual offences such as illicit images and online grooming. DoS, defacing and malware are cyber-dependent.

q: Which of the following are examples of cyber-dependent crime?
explain: Cyber-dependent crimes are hacking, defacing a website, DoS and malware.

q: Which of the following are listed as cyber-enabled crime?
options: Economic crime - fraud, piracy, IP theft, forgery
Child sexual offences - illicit images, online grooming
Offenses against a specific target - cyberstalking
Online marketplaces for illegal items - drugs, guns, slaves
explain: Slide 9 lists these six categories of crime transformed by technology.

q: Which statements about penetration testing under CMA 1990 are correct?
options: It can use hardware/software hacking, social engineering or any mix
It needs an authorisation letter from a genuine high level manager who has the authority to give it
No authorisation is needed if the tester is a reputable company
Only a VERY limited number of people in the organisation need to know
It is where an AUTHORISED person attempts to gain access to a computer system or data
It can prove that a system is safe
Everyone in the organisation must be told in advance
explain: Pen testing uses an authorised person and cannot "PROVE" a system safe. It can use hardware, software or social engineering, only a very limited number of people need to know, it needs an authorisation letter, and you should use a reputable organisation.

q: Which statements about penetration testing are correct?
options: It is lawful whenever the tester intends no harm
The tester must have an authorisation letter and be present to verify it
It is important to use a reputable organisation (e.g. your auditor?)
A penetration test cannot 'PROVE' a system safe
A passed test proves the system is secure
The authorisation can come from any employee
explain: The authorisation letter comes from a genuine high level manager, and the tester must be present to verify it. Use a reputable organisation, and remember a test cannot "PROVE" a system safe.

q: Which of the following bodies are listed as professional bodies in the cyber security lecture?
explain: Slides 22-25 list NCCU, GCHQ, NCSC, ICO, NIST, OWASP and CREST as professional bodies.

q: Which professional bodies are responsible to prevent cyber threat and reduce cybercrime in the UK?
explain: The NCCU responds to threats and reduces cyber crime. GCHQ protects the UK and defends Government systems. The NCSC protects UK critical services. NIST is a US agency, and OWASP supports application security.

q: What is the job of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC)?
options: Improve the security of the UK Internet
Protect UK critical services from cyber attacks
Respond to threats as the police
Defend Government systems from cyber threat
explain: The NCSC's job is to protect UK critical services from cyber attacks, manage major incidents and improve the security of the UK Internet.

q: What is the job of GCHQ?
options: Improve the security of the UK Internet
Defend Government systems from cyber threat
Collaborate with partners to reduce cyber crime
Protect the UK (with law enforcement and other intelligence agencies)
Test and set standards for technology
explain: GCHQ protects the UK and defends Government systems from cyber threat. The other items belong to NCSC and NCCU.

q: Which statements about the National Cyber Crime Unit are correct?
options: It is an independent authority for DPA/GDPR breaches
They work with Regional Organised Crime Units (ROCUs)
It is part of the National Crime Agency (NCA)
Its job is to respond to threats and collaborate with partners to reduce cyber crime
explain: The National Cyber Crime Unit is the police, is part of the NCA, works with ROCUs, responds to threats and collaborates with partners.

q: Which statements about NIST are correct?
options: It tests and sets standards for technology including security
It is part of the National Crime Agency
It stands for National Institute for Standards and Technology
It is a non-regulatory US agency
It is a UK independent authority
explain: NIST is a non-regulatory US agency that tests and sets standards for technology including security.

q: Which bodies are listed as offering research, pen-testing and education?
explain: OWASP does research, pen-testing and education. CREST does research, pen-testing and education, with "CyberEssentials".

q: Which statements about OWASP and CREST are correct?
options: OWASP is a global not-for-profit supporting application security
CREST is a not-for-profit representing the information security industry
OWASP is a US regulatory agency
Both offer research, pen-testing and education
CREST is a UK police unit
explain: OWASP and CREST are both not-for-profit with research, pen-testing, education.

q: 'Hacking' may also be an offence against which of the following?
options: Data Protection Act 1998 [some civil + some criminal offences]
Other legislation and/or contract of employment
explain: 'Hacking' may also be an offence against the CMA 1990, the DPA 1998, other legislation and/or contract of employment.

q: Which laws are listed against cyber-dependent crimes?
explain: Cyber-dependent crimes slide lists these three Acts.

q: Which penalty statements for CMA 1990 offences are correct?
explain: Slide 12 gives penalties of 2 years for S1, previously 6 months, 5 years for S2 and 10 years for S3.

q: Which statements comparing ethics and law are correct?
options: Laws carry the authority of a governing body
Laws are rules that mandate or prohibit certain behaviour
Ethics can be universal, laws tend to be local
Ethics come from moral attitudes or customs
explain: All statements are from slide 4.

q: Which statements comparing ethics and law are correct?
options: Laws are not drawn from ethics
Laws carry the authority of a governing body
Ethics come from moral attitudes or customs
Laws come from moral attitudes or customs
Ethics carry the authority of a governing body
explain: Laws are drawn from ethics and carry the authority of a governing body, and ethics come from moral attitudes or customs.

q: Which statements about terms and conditions (T&Cs) are correct?
options: They protect a company's copyright or licenses
They set out fair use of the product
explain: T&Cs protect a company through fair use of the product, protection of copyright or licenses, and outlining user and company expectations. T&Cs are legally binding.

q: Why does a software developer need to care about computer law?
options: You may need to advise others as to what is legal (or illegal)
You may need to incorporate (or omit) features such as 'authorised users only' at login
Because developers are exempt from the Computer Misuse Act
Because only lawyers are bound by computer law
You may need to incorporate appropriate security and audit trails
You may need to seek further advice (and understand that advice)
explain: Computer law matters because you may need to incorporate or omit features, add security and audit trails, advise others and seek further advice.

q: Which statements about Sarbanes Oxley (SOX) are correct?
options: Company directors must provide the correct information to auditors
US public companies must establish 'hotlines' to enable employees to anonymously raise concerns about accounting or audit irregularities
It sets standards for storing card holder data
It is the UK law criminalising hacking
explain: SOX requires hotlines and requires directors to give correct information to auditors. EuroSOX is the EU equivalent.

q: Which statements about PCI DSS compliance are correct?
options: A merchant of any size that accepts credit cards must comply with PCI Security Council standards
If you lose card data you must declare it to the ICO
Lost card data must be reported to the NCA
Compliance is the responsibility of the third party processor only
Compliant means you are doing your best to keep customer's data safe, regardless of whether a third party processes it
explain: PCI DSS slides 16 and 19.

q: Which statements about hacker types are correct?
options: Black hat attackers are authorised to test systems
Black hat attackers are unethical criminals who violate security for personal gain or malicious reasons
Gray hat attackers always report vulnerabilities
Gray hat attackers are somewhere between white and black hat attackers
White hat attackers break into systems to discover weaknesses in order to improve security
White hat attackers attack networks for personal gain
explain: Slide 13.

q: Which statements about the Computer Misuse Act 1990 section scope are correct?
options: Section 3ZA covers unauthorised acts causing, or creating risk of, serious damage
Section 1 covers unauthorised access to computer material
Section 1 covers acts causing serious damage
Section 3A covers making, supplying or obtaining articles for use in an offence under section 1, 2, 3 or 3ZA
Section 2 covers unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences
Section 3 covers making articles for use in offences
explain: Slide 10 section list.

q: Which statements about cybercrime are correct?
options: Cyber-dependent crimes can be committed only through the use of ICT devices
It describes two closely linked but distinct criminal activities
Cyber-enabled crimes can be committed only through ICT devices
Cyber-enabled crimes are traditional crimes increased in scale or reach by ICT
Cyber-dependent crimes are traditional crimes increased in reach by ICT
explain: Cybercrime is cyber-dependent crime plus cyber-enabled crime, according to the UK Government in 2016.
